# TYSON FOODS, INC. (TSN)
Analysis date: 2026-11-16

## Overview

- Tyson is a world‑class food company with a broad portfolio of iconic brands and about 124,000 team members worldwide — 10-K line 130: Tyson Foods, Inc. and its subsidiaries (collectively, the “Company,” “we,” “us,” “our,” “Tyson”) ... had approximately 124,000 employees (“team members”) on October 3, 2026.
- The company operates a fully vertically integrated chicken production process that spans breeding, feed, hatchery, grow‑out, processing and distribution — 10-K line 132: We operate a fully vertically integrated chicken production process.
- Tyson also processes live cattle and hogs into dressed meat, case‑ready products and specialty items — 10-K line 133: We also process live fed cattle and hogs and fabricate dressed beef and pork carcasses into primal and sub‑primal meat cuts, case‑ready beef and pork and fully cooked meats.
- A dedicated venture subsidiary invests in innovative protein, animal‑welfare and sustainability technologies — 10-K line 135: Tyson New Ventures, LLC is used to broaden our exposure to innovative forms of protein and opportunities to improve animal welfare, water management, packaging and land stewardship...

## Market Positioning and Growth Outlook

- Tyson competes globally with other food producers and seeks market leadership through advertising, price, product safety, brand strength and innovation — 10-K line 171: Our food products compete with those of other food producers and processors and certain prepared food manufacturers.
- The principal competitive elements include advertising, consumer and trade promotions, price, product safety and quality, brand identification, innovation, breadth and depth of product offerings, availability of products, customer service and credit terms — 10-K line 175: The principal competitive elements are advertising, consumer and trade promotions, price, product safety and quality, brand identification, innovation, breadth and depth of product offerings, availability of products, customer service and credit terms.
- Walmart represents the largest single customer, contributing roughly nineteen percent of consolidated sales; no other customer exceeds ten percent — 10-K line 169: Walmart Inc. accounted for approximately 19.0% of our fiscal 2026 consolidated sales. ... No other single customer or customer group represented more than 10% of fiscal 2026 consolidated sales.
- Tyson markets products in roughly one hundred forty countries and regions, with major sales markets across North America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East — 10-K line 177: We sold products in approximately 140 countries and regions in fiscal 2026.
- Management expects domestic protein production to be flat to slightly higher in fiscal 2027, providing a neutral to modestly positive supply backdrop — EX-99.1 line 112: For fiscal 2027, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) indicates domestic protein production (beef, pork, chicken and turkey) will be flat to a slight increase compared to fiscal 2026 levels.
- Liquidity is projected to stay well above the company’s minimum target, supporting operations and strategic initiatives — EX-99.1 line 134: We expect total liquidity, which was $4.1 billion as of October 3, 2026, to remain well above our minimum liquidity target of $1.0 billion.
Insight: Tyson’s fully vertically integrated chicken model gives it control over breeding, feed, processing and distribution, a capability highlighted by its claim "We operate a fully vertically integrated chicken production process" — 10-K line 132.

## Valuation Insights

The 10‑K filing covers the full fiscal year that ended on October 3 2026, with comparable prior‑year data for the year ended September 27 2025. The earnings release presents twelve‑month results that align with the same fiscal period, noting that the fourth quarter contained an extra week which was adjusted out for non‑GAAP measures.
Revenue for the year was reported as modestly higher than the prior year, reflecting overall growth despite legal contingency adjustments that reduced the topline in both years.
Operating income for the year was essentially unchanged from the prior year, indicating flat profitability at the GAAP level.
GAAP earnings per share were slightly lower than the prior year, while adjusted earnings per share showed a more pronounced decline, highlighting the impact of the additional week and other non‑GAAP adjustments.
Operating margin, as disclosed in the release, was low, consistent with the thin profitability typical of a high‑volume, low‑margin food‑production business.
The company generated positive cash from operations and free cash flow, with free cash flow derived by subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash flow, as defined in the non‑GAAP reconciliation.
Total stockholders’ equity declined modestly year over year, providing a basis for return‑on‑equity calculations, though the resulting return was described as low.
Long‑term debt figures were not disclosed in the provided data set, so leverage ratios such as debt‑to‑equity or net‑debt‑to‑EBITDA cannot be computed or evaluated.
No market price for the common stock, price date, or price source was supplied; consequently, valuation multiples that rely on a price denominator (e.g., price‑to‑earnings) are unavailable, and any assessment of valuation limits must be qualified accordingly.
Peer data were not supplied, therefore comparative analysis against industry peers cannot be performed within the constraints of the available evidence.
The filing indicates a change in segment reporting: the International segment, previously non‑reportable, was elevated to a reportable segment beginning in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, which affects segment‑level profitability analysis.

## Future Developments and Strategic Recommendations

- Tyson conducts continuous research and development, including new product innovation, ingredient simplification, automation and breeding stock improvements — 10-K line 182: We conduct continuous research and development activities which include new product innovation, product improvements, ingredient simplification, manual process automation in our processing facilities and grow‑out operations and chicken breeding stock improvements.
- The company’s network optimization plan is a key catalyst, but its success depends on efficient implementation and may incur multi‑year costs — 10-K line 234: The success of our network optimization plan, or any other financial or operational optimization plans, will depend in part on our ability to successfully implement them in an efficient and effective manner.
- Disease outbreaks such as African swine fever or highly pathogenic avian influenza could materially affect livestock supply, product demand and brand perception — 10-K line 225: Supply of and demand for our products can be adversely impacted by disease outbreaks impacting animals, animal products and livestock, such as African swine fever (“ASF”), bovine spongiform encephalopathy, foot and mouth disease, highly pathogenic avian influenza (“HPAI”)...
- Fluctuations in commodity and feed‑grain prices can erode gross margins and limit the ability to pass costs to customers — 10-K line 219: Fluctuations in commodity prices and in the availability of raw materials, especially feed grains, live cattle, live swine and other inputs, could negatively impact our earnings.
- Intensifying competition and private‑label pressure may force price concessions or higher promotional spending, weighing on profitability — 10-K line 224: The food industry in general is intensely competitive. We face competition from other food producers and processors ... From time to time, in response to competitive pressures or to maintain market share, we may need to reduce the prices for some of our products...
- Climate‑change risks could raise input costs, disrupt production and require additional capital expenditures — 10-K line 291: Climate change may have a long‑term adverse impact on our business.
- Judgment: Maintain and expand R&D investment to sustain product innovation and mitigate competitive pressure — 10-K line 182: We conduct continuous research and development activities which include new product innovation, product improvements, ingredient simplification, manual process automation in our processing facilities and grow‑out operations and chicken breeding stock improvements.
- Judgment: Prioritize execution of the network optimization plan while monitoring cost overruns, as management warns that implementation may be more difficult, costly or time‑consuming than expected — 10-K line 234: The success of our network optimization plan, or any other financial or operational optimization plans, will depend in part on our ability to successfully implement them in an efficient and effective manner.

## Investment Recommendation

**Hold** — Tyson Foods leverages a fully vertically integrated chicken operation and a broad portfolio of iconic brands to sustain its market presence across domestic and international markets. The company generates positive cash from operations and maintains liquidity well above its minimum target, providing flexibility for strategic initiatives. However, operating profitability remains low and essentially flat year over year, reflecting thin margins typical of high‑volume food production and exposure to commodity price swings, disease risks, and competitive pricing pressures. Without clearer evidence of margin expansion or transformational growth from the network optimization plan, the balanced outlook supports a neutral stance.
Deciding metric unavailable; the recommendation cannot be assessed against its selected calculation.
- Risk: Commodity and feed‑grain price volatility that can erode gross margins
- Risk: Disease outbreaks such as avian influenza or swine fever that could disrupt supply and demand
- Risk: Intensifying competition and private‑label pressure that may force price concessions
- Risk: Uncertain financial impact of the multi‑year network optimization plan
- Risk: Climate‑related cost pressures and regulatory changes
Insight: unavailable; no supported investment insight was supplied.

## Evidence gaps

- No specific quantitative guidance for segment volume growth or price trends beyond the general USDA outlook and liquidity statement.
- The filing does not provide detailed timelines or capital allocation amounts for upcoming innovation projects beyond the broad R&D description.
- There is no disclosed metric on the expected impact of AI or emerging technologies on operating efficiency; only risk statements are provided.
- Missing long‑term debt data prevents calculation of leverage metrics and assessment of debt service capacity.
- Absent stock price information precludes computation of market‑based valuation multiples such as price‑to‑earnings or enterprise value ratios.
- Lack of peer financials means no benchmarking can be conducted to contextualize the company’s margins, growth rates, or return metrics.

## Audit appendix

- Valuation Insights section is absent – required analysis of valuation multiples, implied price targets, and sensitivity is missing.
- Capital‑expenditure outlook is not quantified; the filing only mentions ongoing projects (line 367) without a forward‑looking spend figure.
- Long‑term debt data are unavailable, preventing calculation of leverage ratios (debt‑to‑equity, interest coverage).
- Peer‑company financial metrics are not supplied, so benchmarking and relative valuation cannot be performed.

Based on analysis of our assessment in accordance with guidance related to unrecognized tax benefits, we have not recorded a liability related to our assessment. Additionally, the purchaser in the transaction also received an assessment from the Mexican tax authorities related to the sale of the indirect equity interest, which was affirmed in January 2025 by a circuit court in Mexico, but remains subject to potential further judicial review under a petition filed by the purchaser. The transaction agreement contains certain mutual indemnification provisions, and both parties provided notice of indemnification claims to the other party. On November 14, 2025, we settled the indemnification provision and entered into an agreement in which the purchaser agreed to assume all tax liabilities in connection with our assessment, assume defense of such assessment and waive all potential indemnification claims against the Company. 459: Our business operations give rise to certain market risk exposures mostly due to changes in commodity prices, foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates. We manage a portion of these risks through the use of derivative financial instruments to reduce our exposure to commodity price risk, foreign currency risk and interest rate risk. Our risk management programs are periodically reviewed by our Board of Directors’ Audit Committee. These programs and risks are monitored by senior management and may be revised as market conditions dictate. Our current risk management programs utilize various industry-standard models that take into account the implicit cost of hedging. Credit risks associated with our derivative contracts are not significant, as we minimize counterparty exposure by dealing with credit-worthy counterparties and utilizing exchange-traded instruments, margin accounts or letters of credit. Additionally, our derivative contracts are mostly short-term in duration, and we generally do not make use of credit-risk-related contingent features. No significant concentrations of credit risk existed at June 27, 2026.
468: We recognize all derivative instruments as either assets or liabilities at fair value in the Consolidated Condensed Balance Sheets, with the exception of normal purchases and normal sales expected to result in physical delivery. For those derivative instruments that are designated and qualify as hedging instruments, we designate the hedging instrument based upon the exposure being hedged (e.g., cash flow hedge or fair value hedge). We designate certain forward contracts as follows:
469: •Cash Flow Hedges – include certain commodity forward and option contracts of forecasted purchases (e.g., grains), interest rate swaps and locks and certain foreign exchange forward contracts
471: Cash Flow Hedges
472: Derivative instruments are designated as hedges against changes in the amount of future cash flows related to procurement of certain commodities utilized in our production processes as well as interest rates on our variable rate debt. For the derivative instruments we designate and qualify as a cash flow hedge, the gain or loss on the derivative is reported as a component of other comprehensive income (“OCI”) and reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods during which the hedged transaction affects earnings. Based on market prices as of June 27, 2026, we have net pretax losses of $4 million for our commodity contracts, which are expected to be reclassified into earnings within the next twelve months. Additionally, we have $8 million of realized losses related to treasury rate locks in connection with the issuance of the 2029 and 2048 Notes, which will be reclassified to earnings over the lives of these notes. During the three and nine months ended June 27, 2026 and June 28, 2025, we did not reclassify significant pretax gains or losses into earnings as a result of the discontinuance of cash flow hedges. For the derivative instruments we designate and qualify as a fair value hedge, the gain or loss on the derivative, as well as the offsetting gain or loss on the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk, are recognized in earnings in the same period. We include the gain or loss on the hedged items (e.g., livestock purchase firm commitments) in the same line item, Cost of Sales, as the offsetting gain or loss on the related livestock forward position. 249: Non-GAAP Financial Measures
250: Adjusted Sales (due to the impact of an additional week in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026), Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Income before Income Taxes, Adjusted Income Tax Expense, Adjusted Net Income Attributable to Tyson and Adjusted EPS, EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, net debt to EBITDA, net debt to Adjusted EBITDA, Segment Operating Income (Loss), As Adjusted, Corporate Expenses, As Adjusted, Amortization, As Adjusted, and Free Cash Flow are presented as supplemental financial measures in the evaluation of our business that are not required by, or presented in accordance with GAAP. The non-GAAP financial measures are tools intended to assist our management and investors in comparing our performance on a consistent basis for purposes of business decision-making by removing the impact of certain items that management believes do not directly reflect our core operations on an ongoing basis. These non-GAAP measures should not be a substitute for their comparable GAAP financial measures. Investors should rely primarily on our GAAP results and use non-GAAP financial measures only supplementally in making investment decisions. We believe the presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures helps management and investors to assess our operating performance from period to period, including our ability to generate earnings sufficient to service our debt, enhances understanding of our financial performance and highlights operational trends. These measures are widely used by investors and rating agencies in the valuation, comparison, rating and investment recommendations of companies. Our calculation of non-GAAP measures may not be comparable to similarly titled measures reported by other companies and other companies may not define these non-GAAP financial measures in the same way, which may limit their usefulness as comparative measures.
251: Definitions
252: EBITDA is defined as net income (loss) before interest, income taxes, depreciation and amortization. Net debt to EBITDA (Adjusted EBITDA) represents the ratio of our debt, net of cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, to EBITDA (and to Adjusted EBITDA). EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, net debt to EBITDA and net debt to Adjusted EBITDA are presented as supplemental financial measurements in the evaluation of our business.
253: Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Income before Income Taxes, Adjusted Income Tax Expense, Adjusted Net Income Attributable to Tyson and Adjusted EPS are defined as EBITDA, Operating Income (Loss), Income (Loss) before Income Taxes, Income Tax Expense (Benefit), Net Income (Loss) Attributable to Tyson and diluted earnings per share, respectively, excluding the impacts of any items that management believes do not directly reflect our core operations on an ongoing basis, as well as the impact of an additional week in fiscal 2026.
254: Adjusted Sales is defined as reported Sales excluding the impact of the additional week in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. The impact of the additional week is calculated by dividing the fourth quarter reported Sales, excluding legal contingency accruals recognized as a reduction to Sales that were not impacted by the additional week, by 14 weeks. We believe Adjusted Sales is a useful measure as it improves period-to-period comparability of sales when a fiscal year includes a 53-week accounting cycle.
255: Segment Operating Income (Loss) is defined as Operating Income (Loss) excluding corporate expenses and amortization. Corporate expenses are unallocated general and administrative costs, including the costs of corporate functions, that are shared across multiple segments. Amortization includes amortization from intangible assets, including brands and trademarks, customer relationships, supply arrangements, patents and intellectual property and land use rights, as well as amortization of software.
256: Segment Operating Income (Loss), As Adjusted is defined as Segment Operating Income (Loss) excluding items affecting comparability, which in management’s judgment, affect the period-to-period assessment of operating results. Items affecting comparability include restructuring and related charges (including network optimization), plant closure and disposal charges (net of gains), goodwill and intangible impairments, brand and product line discontinuations, facility fire related costs (net of insurance proceeds) and certain non-ordinary course legal, regulatory and other matters, as well as the impact of an additional week in fiscal 2026.
257: Corporate Expenses, As Adjusted is defined as Corporate Expenses excluding items affecting comparability, which in management’s judgment, affect the period-to-period assessment of operating results. Items affecting comparability include restructuring and related charges (including network optimization), corporate asset disposal charges (net of gains) and certain non-ordinary course legal, regulatory and other matters, as well as the impact of an additional week in fiscal 2026.
258: Amortization, As Adjusted is defined as Amortization excluding the impact of items affecting comparability, which in management’s judgment, affect the period-to-period assessment of operating results. Items affecting comparability include accelerated amortization related to the discontinuance of intangible assets, as well as the impact of an additional week in fiscal 2026.

117: Principal Accountant Fees and Services
128: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
130: Tyson Foods, Inc. and its subsidiaries (collectively, the “Company,” “we,” “us,” “our,” “Tyson Foods” or “Tyson”) (NYSE: TSN) is a world-class food company and recognized leader in protein. Founded in 1935 by John W. Tyson, it has grown under four generations of family leadership. The Company is guided by its core values and unified by this purpose: Tyson Foods. We Feed the World Like Family™ and has a broad portfolio of iconic products and brands including Tyson®, Jimmy Dean®, Hillshire Farm®, Ball Park®, Wright®, State Fair®, aidells® and ibp®. Tyson Foods is dedicated to bringing high-quality food to every table in the world, safely and affordably, now and for future generations. Headquartered in Springdale, Arkansas, the Company had approximately 124,000 employees (“team members”) on October 3, 2026. Through its core values, Tyson Foods strives to operate with integrity, create value for its shareholders, customers, communities and team members, be faith-friendly and inclusive, provide a safe work environment and serve as a steward of the animals, land and environment entrusted to it.
131: Some of the key factors influencing our business are customer demand for our products; ability to maintain and grow relationships with customers and introduce new and innovative products to the marketplace; accessibility of international markets; market prices for our products; cost and availability of live cattle and hogs, raw materials and feed ingredients; availability of team members to operate our production facilities; and operating efficiencies of our facilities.
132: We operate a fully vertically integrated chicken production process. Our integrated operations consist of breeding stock, contract farmers, feed production, processing, further processing, marketing and transportation of chicken and related specialty products, including animal and pet food ingredients. Through our wholly owned subsidiary, Cobb-Vantress, we are one of the leading poultry breeding stock suppliers in the world. Investments in breeding stock research and development enable us to breed into our flocks the characteristics found to be most desirable.
133: We also process live fed cattle and hogs and fabricate dressed beef and pork carcasses into primal and sub-primal meat cuts, case-ready beef and pork and fully cooked meats. In addition, we derive value from specialty products such as hides and variety meats sold to further processors and others.
134: We produce a wide range of fresh, value-added, frozen and refrigerated food products. Our products are marketed and sold primarily by our sales staff to grocery retailers, grocery wholesalers, meat distributors, warehouse club stores, military commissaries, industrial food processing companies, chain restaurants or their distributors, live markets, international export companies and domestic distributors who serve restaurants, foodservice operations such as plant and school cafeterias, convenience stores, hospitals and other vendors. Additionally, sales to the military and a portion of sales to international markets are made through independent brokers and trading companies.
135: As part of our commitment to innovation and growth, we have a subsidiary focused on investing in companies developing innovative technologies, business models and products that have the potential to transform the food industry. Tyson New Ventures, LLC is used to broaden our exposure to innovative forms of protein and opportunities to improve animal welfare, water management, packaging and land stewardship to complement the Company’s continuing investments in innovation in our Beef, Pork, Chicken, Prepared Foods and International businesses.
138: Our President and Chief Executive Officer is the Chief Operating Decision Maker (“CODM”) of the Company. Commencing in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, we no longer allocate corporate expenses and amortization to our segments as these items are no longer used by our CODM in assessing the performance of, and allocating resources to, the segments. Segment operating income (loss) is now defined as Operating Income (Loss) excluding corporate expenses and amortization to reflect these changes. Corporate expenses are unallocated general and administrative costs, including the costs of corporate functions, that are shared across multiple segments. Amortization includes amortization of intangible assets, including brands and trademarks, customer relationships, supply arrangements, patents and intellectual property and land use rights, as well as amortization of software.
139: All prior period amounts have been recast to reflect the new presentation of segment operating income (loss). The contribution of each segment to consolidated sales and operating income (loss), and the identifiable assets attributable to each segment, are set forth in Part II, Item 8, Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 17: Segment Reporting.
149: Prepared Foods includes our operations related to manufacturing and marketing frozen and refrigerated food products and logistics operations to move products through the supply chain. This segment includes brands such as Jimmy Dean®, Hillshire Farm®, Ball Park®, Wright® and State Fair®, as well as the artisanal brands aidells® and Gallo Salame®. Products primarily include a mixture of ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat sandwiches, sandwich components such as flame-grilled hamburgers and Philly steaks, pepperoni, bacon, breakfast sausage, turkey, lunchmeat, hot dogs, flour and corn tortilla products, appetizers, snacks, prepared meals, ethnic foods, side dishes, meat dishes, breadsticks and processed meats. Products are marketed domestically to food retailers, foodservice distributors, restaurant operators, convenience stores, hotel chains and noncommercial foodservice establishments such as schools, healthcare facilities, the military and other food processors, as well as to international export markets.
151: International includes our foreign operations in China, Europe, Malaysia, Mexico, South Korea, Thailand and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia related to raising and processing live chickens into and purchasing raw materials for fresh, frozen and value-added chicken products, as well as the distribution of chicken products and other protein and non-protein food products. Products are marketed to foodservice distributors and retailers and to other international markets.
154: The primary raw material used in our beef operations is live cattle. We do not own cattle-raising facilities but employ cattle buyers located throughout cattle-producing regions who purchase live cattle on the open spot market from independent feedyards and public auctions. These buyers are trained to select high-quality animals, and we continually measure their performance. We also enter into various risk-sharing and procurement arrangements with producers to secure a supply of livestock for our facilities. Although we generally expect adequate supply of live cattle in the regions we operate, there may be periods of imbalance in supply and demand. The United States cattle market is currently experiencing a limited supply of market-ready cattle, and uncertainty exists regarding the timing of the cattle herd rebuilding.
159: The primary raw materials used in our domestic chicken operations are corn and soybean meal used as feed and live chickens raised primarily by independent contract farmers. Our vertically integrated chicken process begins with breeding our pedigree and great-grandparent stock to produce grandparent breeder flocks and ends with broilers for processing. Breeder flocks (i.e., grandparents) are raised to maturity in grandparent growing and laying farms where fertile eggs are produced. Fertile eggs are incubated at the grandparent hatchery and produce pullets (i.e., parents). Pullets are raised to 20 weeks of age, sent to breeder houses, and the resulting eggs are sent to our hatcheries. Once chicks have hatched, they are sent to broiler farms. There, contract farmers care for and raise the chicks according to our standards, with support from our technical service personnel, until the broilers reach the desired processing weight. Adult chickens are transported to processing facilities where they are harvested and converted into finished products, which are then sent to distribution centers and delivered to customers.
165: The primary raw materials used in our international operations are live chickens, feed ingredients for chickens we raise and ingredients used in the production and distribution of fresh, frozen and value-added chicken products and other protein and non-protein food products. Some of these raw materials are provided by our other segments, while most are purchased from numerous suppliers and manufacturers. We believe the sources of supply of raw materials are adequate for our present needs.
167: Demand for beef, chicken, pork and certain prepared foods products, such as hot dogs and smoked sausage, generally increases during the spring and summer months and other key holiday periods and is generally softer during the winter months. Other prepared foods products, such as prepared meals, meat dishes, appetizers, bacon and breakfast sausage, generally experience increased demand during the winter months and key holiday periods, while demand is generally softer during the spring and summer months.
168: CUSTOMERS
169: Walmart Inc. accounted for approximately 19.0% of our fiscal 2026 consolidated sales. Sales to Walmart Inc. were included in all of our segments. Any extended discontinuance of sales to this customer could, if not replaced, have a material impact on our operations. No other single customer or customer group represented more than 10% of fiscal 2026 consolidated sales.
170: COMPETITION
171: Our food products compete with those of other food producers and processors and certain prepared food manufacturers. Additionally, our food products compete in markets around the world. We seek to achieve a leading market position for our products through our principal marketing and competitive strategy, which includes:
172: •identifying target markets for value-added products;
174: •utilizing our national distribution systems and customer support services.
175: Past efforts indicate customer demand can be increased and sustained through our marketing strategy, strong consumer insights and market analytics and our national distribution systems. The principal competitive elements are advertising, consumer and trade promotions, price, product safety and quality, brand identification, innovation, breadth and depth of product offerings, availability of products, customer service and credit terms.
177: We sold products in approximately 140 countries and regions in fiscal 2026. Major sales markets include Canada, Central America, China, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan, Mexico, Malaysia, the Middle East, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
179: We have foreign operations in our Chicken and International segments. Cobb-Vantress, a chicken breeding stock subsidiary in our Chicken segment, has business interests in Argentina, Brazil, China, the Dominican Republic, India, New Zealand, Peru, the Philippines, Spain, Tanzania, Turkey and the United Kingdom. Our International segment includes our chicken production operations in China and Thailand, as well as multiprotein further-processing operations in China, Malaysia, South Korea and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. 204: We have the ability to produce and ship fresh, frozen and refrigerated products worldwide. Domestically, our distribution system extends to a broad network of food distributors and is supported by our owned or leased cold storage warehouses, public cold storage facilities and our transportation system. Our distribution centers accumulate fresh and frozen products so we can fill and consolidate partial-truckload orders into full truckloads, thereby decreasing shipping costs while improving customer service. In addition, we provide our customers a wide selection of products that do not require large volume orders. Our distribution system enables us to supply large or small quantities of products to meet customer requirements anywhere in the continental United States. Internationally, we utilize both rail and truck refrigerated transportation to domestic ports, where products are consolidated for shipment to international destinations.
